title: Vital Statistics
text:
Looking for a handy overview of employment, business activity, housing, population, and crime in Waterloo Region? This Vital Statistics page is where to look. It contains a regularly updated collection of charts on the Region’s health in each of these key areas, often with Ontario and Canada added for comparison. Most of the data used to produce these charts is updated monthly, so this page will be refreshed at least once a month to capture the latest statistics. The rental, population, and crime data is released annually, so those charts will only change once a year. The data in many of these charts will also be analyzed in more depth in regular posts.
The population and crime charts include data for the entire Region, but for all other charts, only data for the Kitchener-Cambridge-Waterloo census metropolitan area (CMA) is available. The CMA covers the Region excluding Wellesley Township. Wellesley contains only 1.7% of the Region’s population, so its exclusion from the data has no meaningful impact on the statistics in these charts. As such, the term “Region” is used throughout the charts on this page.
All charts are interactive, so hovering over any line or bar shows a box with details of the underlying data point.
See Key terms for definitions.
Unless otherwise indicated, this legend applies to all charts on this page.

NoteKey terms









Term
Definition




Active businesses
“Active businesses are those businesses that reported having one or more employees in a given month.” (Statistics Canada, table 33-10-0270-01, footnote 4)


Apartment
“all dwellings other than those described above, including structures commonly known as stacked townhouses, duplexes, triplexes, double duplexes and row duplexes.” (CMHC, Survey methodologies: Starts and Completions and Market Absorption, “Apartment and Other”)


Average rent
“The rent refers to the actual amount tenants pay for their unit. No adjustments are made for the inclusion or exclusion of amenities and services.” (CMHC, Methodology for Rental Market Survey)


Condo
“an individual dwelling unit which is privately owned, but where the building and/or the land are collectively owned by all dwelling unit owners.” (CMHC, Survey methodologies: Starts and Completions and Market Absorption, “Condominium”)


Crime Severity Index
“The Crime Severity Index (CSI) measures changes in the level of severity of crime in Canada from year to year. In the index, all crimes are assigned a weight based on their seriousness. The level of seriousness is based on actual sentences handed down by the courts in all provinces and territories. More serious crimes are assigned higher weights, less serious offences lower weights.” “The crime severity index includes all Criminal Code violations including traffic, as well as drug violations and all Federal Statutes.” (Statistics Canada, table 35-10-0026-01, footnotes 20 and 16)


Employment
“Number of persons who, during the reference week, worked for pay or profit, or performed unpaid family work or had a job but were not at work due to own illness or disability, personal or family responsibilities, labour dispute, vacation, or other reason. Those persons on layoff and persons without work but who had a job to start at a definite date in the future are not considered employed.” (Statistics Canada, table 14-10-0459-01, footnote 7)


Homeowner
“a residence where the owner owns the dwelling and lot outright.” (CMHC, Survey methodologies: Starts and Completions and Market Absorption)


Housing starts
A start is “the beginning of construction work on a building. This is usually when the concrete has been poured for the whole of the footing around the structure or an equivalent stage where a basement will not be part of the structure.” (CMHC, Survey methodologies: Starts and Completions and Market Absorption)


Immigrant
“Immigrant refers to a person who is, or who has ever been, a permanent resident (landed immigrant). Such a person has been granted the right to live in Canada permanently by immigration authorities. Immigrants who have obtained Canadian citizenship by naturalization are included in this group.” (Statistics Canada)


Incidents
The number of incidents reported to a police service. Unreported crimes are therefore not included in this number.


Interprovincial migration
“Interprovincial migration represents all movement from one province or territory to another involving a change in the usual place [of] residence.” (Statistics Canada, Annual Demographic Estimates: Subprovincial Areas, Appendix A: Glossary)


Intraprovincial migration
“Intraprovincial migration or subprovincial migration represents all movement from one region to another within the same province or territory involving a change of the usual place [of] residence.” (Statistics Canada, Annual Demographic Estimates: Subprovincial Areas, Appendix A: Glossary)


Labour force
“Number of civilian, non-institutionalized persons 15 years of age and over who, during the reference week, were employed or unemployed.” (Statistics Canada, table 14-10-0459-01, footnote 6)


Natural increase in population
“Variation of the population size over a given period as a result of the difference between the numbers of births and deaths.” (Statistics Canada, Annual Demographic Estimates: Subprovincial Areas, Appendix A: Glossary)


New Housing Price Index
“The New Housing Price Index (NHPI) is a monthly series that measures changes over time in the builders’ selling prices of new residential houses, where detailed specifications pertaining to each house remain the same between two consecutive periods.” “The index base period, for which the New Housing Price Index (NHPI) equals 100, is December 2016.” (Statistics Canada, New Housing Price Index survey description; table 18-10-0205-01, footnote 3)


Non-permanent resident
“A non-permanent resident refers to a person from another country with a usual place of residence in Canada and who has a work or study permit or who has claimed refugee status (asylum claimant, protected person or member of related groups). Family members living with work or study permit holders are also included unless these family members are already Canadian citizens, landed immigrants (permanent residents), or non-permanent residents themselves.” (Statistics Canada, table 17-10-0153-01, footnote 13)


Non-violent crime
“The non-violent crime severity index includes all non-violent Criminal Code violations including traffic, as well as drug violations and all Federal Statutes.” (Statistics Canada, table 35-10-0026-01, footnote 19)


Openings
“Opening businesses are businesses that transition from having no employees in the previous month to having at least one employee in the current month. These instances occur when a new, small firm begins, when a large firm opens a new establishment or when a seasonal firm re-opens.” (Statistics Canada, table 33-10-0270-01, footnote 1)


Participation rate
“The participation rate is the number of labour force participants expressed as a percentage of the population 15 years of age and over. The participation rate for a particular group (age, gender, marital status, etcetera.) is the number of labour force participants in that group expressed as a percentage of the population for that group.” (Statistics Canada, table 14-10-0459-01, footnote 10)


Regular beneficiaries
“The number of beneficiaries represents a count of persons who qualified for employment insurance benefits during the Labour Force Survey reference week, usually containing the 15th day of the month.” “Includes people who receive regular income benefits whether or not they participate in one of three employment benefit programs, namely Skills Development Program, Job Creation Partnerships Program and Self-employment Program.” (Statistics Canada, table 14-10-0454-01, footnotes 4 and 1)


Rental
“a dwelling constructed for rental purposes, regardless of who finances the structure.” (CMHC, Survey methodologies: Starts and Completions and Market Absorption)


Row
“a 1-family dwelling unit in a row of 3 or more attached dwellings separated by a common or party wall extending from ground to roof.” (CMHC, Survey methodologies: Starts and Completions and Market Absorption, “Row (Townhouse)”)


Same-sample rent change
“Percentage change in average rent provides an estimate of rent level movement by eliminating the compositional effects of new structures, conversions and survey sample rotation. The estimate is based on existing rental structures that were common to the survey sample for both the previous year and the current Rental Market Survey year.” (CMHC, Methodology for Rental Market Survey)


Semi-detached
“1 of 2 dwellings located side-by-side in a building, adjoining no other structure and separated by a common or party wall extending from ground to roof.” (CMHC, Survey methodologies: Starts and Completions and Market Absorption)


Single-detached
“a building containing 1 dwelling unit, which is completely separated on all sides from any other dwelling or structure.” (CMHC, Survey methodologies: Starts and Completions and Market Absorption, “Single-Detached”)


Unemployment rate
“The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed persons expressed as a percentage of the labour force. The unemployment rate for a particular group (age, gender, marital status, etcetera.) is the number unemployed in that group expressed as a percentage of the labour force for that group.” (Statistics Canada, table 14-10-0459-01, footnote 9)


Vacancy rate
“A unit is considered vacant if, at the time of the survey, the unit is physically unoccupied and available for immediate rental.” The survey covers “all row projects and apartment structures with three or more units” that are “privately initiated”. (CMHC, Methodology for Rental Market Survey)


Violent crime
“The violent crime severity index includes all Incident-based Uniform Crime Reporting Survey (UCR2) violent violations.” (Statistics Canada, table 35-10-0026-01, footnote 18)

Reliability






Items of note




Labour Force Survey: the unemployment, participation, employment and labour-force figures, overall and by age, are estimates from a monthly survey of about 65,000 households, and a CMA’s share of that sample is small; “estimates are based on smaller sample sizes the more detailed the table becomes, which could result in lower data quality”, and estimates below 1,500 people are suppressed. The CMA figures are three-month moving averages, which Statistics Canada publishes to steady them. The overall unemployment rate, participation rate and employment charts draw the Region’s 95% confidence interval from the published standard errors; the tables by age publish none. Seasonally adjusted series have “seasonal movements … eliminated” but still contain irregular movements; the figures by age are not seasonally adjusted, so their lines rise and fall with the seasons. (tables 14-10-0459, 14-10-0458, 14-10-0017)


Labour Force Survey, figures too unreliable to publish: Statistics Canada rates some of the Region’s monthly figures by age F, “too unreliable to be published”; within the five years shown, that is the unemployment rate of people aged 55 to 64 for November 2023, which leaves a gap in the Region’s line on that chart. (table 14-10-0458)


Employment Insurance revisions: “Estimates for the current and previous month are subject to revision”, so the last two months on the chart may change. (table 14-10-0454)


Business openings and closures: these are experimental estimates from payroll records. Statistics Canada flags the Region’s count of active businesses “use with caution” (E) for June 2021 and January 2022; those counts are not used, which leaves gaps in the Region’s lines on the two per-100-businesses charts. The counts of openings and closures are not flagged in the months shown, so the net openings bars have no gaps. The chart’s 12-month average also uses the year before the first month shown, and there the Region’s openings for August 2020 are flagged E and not used, so no average can be worked out for June and July 2021 and the line starts in August 2021. (table 33-10-0270)


Seasonally adjusted building permits: Statistics Canada builds the adjusted totals by adding up adjusted parts (single and multiple dwellings; residential, industrial, commercial and institutional values), leaves a series with “no apparent seasonality” unadjusted, and “at the end of the year, the chronological series adjusted for seasonality are revised”, so past months on the permits charts can change each year. (table 34-10-0292)


Population estimates are revised: the latest year’s population and components are preliminary and the two or three before it updated; each is revised as later data come in, the last when the next census is counted. (tables 17-10-0152, 17-10-0153, 17-10-0155)


Crime Severity Index and incident rates: police-reported crime only; the previous year’s figures are revised each year; the index weights were updated with 2022 data; and some older records were imputed from the aggregate survey. (tables 35-10-0026, 35-10-0177)


Railway police undercount, 2021 and 2022: the “Other Federal Statutes” incidents the Canadian Pacific Railway Police reported for 2021 and 2022 “may be an undercount” and “should be interpreted with caution”. They are part of all violations, so of the overall and non-violent incident rates. (table 35-10-0177)


CMHC housing starts: CMHC counts starts every month in census metropolitan areas and census agglomerations, the centres of 10,000 people or more; smaller places are counted only quarterly, by sample. The Ontario and Canada figures here are for those centres.


CMHC Rental Market Survey: a survey each October of a sample of privately initiated rental apartment and row structures of three or more units, in centres of 10,000 people or more. CMHC rates each figure’s reliability; every figure charted is rated excellent, very good or good.


Rental Market Survey figures not shown: CMHC rates some of the Region’s figures “Fair (Use with Caution)”, or does not publish them, because the sample of units of that size is small. They are left out, which leaves a gap in the Region’s line: the rent change for all units in 2021 and for one-bedroom units in 2024. A unit size is charted only where the Region has at least four usable figures of the five, so there is no chart of the studio vacancy rate, or of the rent change for studios or for units with three or more bedrooms.













NoteReproducibility





Reproduce the page: get the code and the data behind every chart (CSV files, in its data/ folder) from vital-statistics/ on GitHub.

title: Monitoring the Region’s pulse with Vital Statistics
text: Looking for a handy overview of employment, business activity, housing, population, and crime in Waterloo Region? The new Vital Statistics page is where to look. It contains a regularly updated collection of charts on the Region’s health in each of these key areas, often with Ontario and Canada added for comparison. Most of the data used to produce these charts is updated monthly, so the page will be refreshed at least once a month to capture the latest statistics. The rental, population, and crime data is released annually, so those charts will only change once a year. You can find it any time under Vital Statistics in the menu at the top of every page.

title: Monitoring the Region’s pulse with Vital Statistics
text:
What does it track?
The page monitors the Region’s health in seven critical areas:

Labour market: employment, labour force participation, unemployment, and Employment Insurance beneficiaries
Business activity: business openings and closings
Building permits: the value of residential and non-residential permits, and the number of dwelling units they create
Housing: housing starts by type and by ownership, and new housing prices
Rental market: vacancy rates, average rents, and the yearly change in rent
Population: the number of residents, how fast it is growing, and where the growth comes from
Crime: the Crime Severity Index and the number of police-reported incidents

Many of these areas will be analyzed in depth in posts of their own. If there’s a statistic you’d like to see added, email me at greg@chartingwaterlooregion.ca.

title: About
text:
ChartingWaterloo Region
    Learning about life in Waterloo Region, one chart at a time.

title: About
text:
What is it?
Charting Waterloo Region (CWR) is a local blog cobbled together to tell stories about life in Waterloo Region using data from (mostly) open sources. In snapshots—posts with a few charts and some basic analysis that can be read in under five minutes—and the occasional deep dive containing more rigorous analysis, CWR will answer questions from the fundamental to the frivolous. Has crime in the Region gotten worse over the past 25 years? CWR will take a stab at answering that (sorry!). What do the townships have more of, cows or people? CWR will investigate that burning issue as well. Basically, CWR is one guy’s effort to illustrate facts and features of Waterloo Region using well-designed charts built from open data.

title: About
text:
Who writes it?
The “one guy” in question is Greg Berberich. I’m a retired GenXer who was a Chartered Accountant for 30 years (I no longer hold the CA designation), the last 25 of those spent between UW and WLU earning a PhD in accounting, teaching, and doing institutional research. In case it’s not obvious, I really like playing with numbers, so as boring as it may sound to most people, that’s what I spend a lot of time doing. Except for a few years in Vancouver in the mid-90s, I’ve lived in the Region my whole life, the first 25 in Kitchener and since 1997 in Waterloo. CWR is my first blog and is basically me doing a hobby in public.

title: About
text:
Why does it exist?
After years (no kidding!) of procrastination, I’ve decided to start publishing some of my charts and analysis because I have learned a lot of interesting and sometimes startling things from them, so I figure it’s worth sharing some of what I learn with other Region residents who want to know more about where they live. And to my knowledge, aside from Jeff Outhit, who does some excellent data journalism for The Record, there is no local outlet that regularly visualizes data about the Region. CWR exists to help fill this gap.

title: About
section: Where does its data come from?
text:
Where does its data come from?
CWR relies primarily on Statistics Canada tables and government open-data portals for its data, supplemented by data from other sources, most of them publicly available. The “Data sources and reliability” section at the end of each post lists the sources, with their links and licences, where applicable. Notes about data reliability that are critical to the proper interpretation of chart data will also be included in this section.

title: About
text:
Is it independent?
My area of expertise as an accountant was in auditing. An auditor’s most-critical asset is their independence because without it, their opinion is worthless. I therefore take CWR’s independence very seriously. CWR is not funded by or affiliated with any government, public-service body, institution, or any other organization or person that could compromise its independence. All editorial decisions and opinions are mine alone.

title: About
text:
Does it have guiding principles?
Yes. Because I’m sharing charts and analysis with the public, I believe I have an obligation to earn readers’ trust, so CWR operates with a few key principles. I’ve read a literal shelf-load of books on data visualization. One called How Charts Lie by data journalist Alberto Cairo sets out several useful charting principles. I’ve adapted a few to guide CWR:

Charts will be based on reliable data.
Charts will not intentionally mislead and will aim not to mislead by accident.
Charts rarely serve as convincing arguments on their own, so they will be supplemented by honest, insightful analysis.
Charts show only what they show, so accompanying analysis will strive not to overstate their implications. Readers should do the same.
Charts will enhance our understanding of their subject matter and start conversations, not stop them.

CWR will also be free of pies and donuts. I love eating them, but they are bad for your charts.

title: About
text:
How is it built?
I use R, a popular language for doing data science, to produce CWR’s charts and tables, and to prepare the data behind them. Quarto combines the R code with my writing and renders it into the HTML, CSS, and images needed to produce the CWR website. These website elements get pushed to a GitHub folder and then served to you via GitHub Pages.
GoatCounter counts page views and post likes so I know which posts people find interesting. The site sets no cookies and records nothing that identifies you, so there is nothing to opt out of.

title: About
text:
Does it use AI?
Yes, I use Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, primarily as the supplier of the code used to modify the site’s infrastructure, to extract and transform the data, and to create the charts, although I do a lot of data-related coding myself (it’s fun!).
I make all editorial and design decisions, from the look and features of the site to the questions I answer, the analysis I do, and the charts I use, sometimes with Claude as a consultant. Claude also assists with background research, helping me identify sources, summarize lengthy documents, and synthesize content to provide useful context for my own analysis. I audit what Claude produces to ensure it’s relevant and reliable.
I write the analysis and discussion in each post, including the chart titles and subtitles, with Claude serving as a copy editor to help me clean up and refine the post for publication. Every statistic in a post’s text and every data point in its charts is taken from the data by code, and all of that code is public (see next section), so you can check any of it for accuracy. Claude drafts the charts’ alt text for screen readers, the Sources sections, each post’s README, and the data dictionary, then I review and edit them before posting. I take full responsibility for the final product and credit all sources used to produce it.

title: About
text:
Is it reproducible?
Yes, if you are so inclined, you can reproduce every post using the code and data in its associated GitHub folder. If you just want a post’s data, you can download a zip file containing the tables in CSV and Parquet formats, as well as an Excel workbook (when the tables are small enough), and a brief data dictionary describing the fields in each table. The “Reproducibility and data download” section at the end of each post contains links to the post’s GitHub folder and zipped data files.

title: About
text:
Can its content be reused?
Yes, everything on CWR is reusable, apart from material quoted from other sources, which stays under its owner’s terms. The text and charts are published under CC BY 4.0, so they can be copied, shared, or republished, including in the news, as long as CWR receives credit. And all the code is MIT licensed, so it can be reused as well. All data stays under the terms set by whoever published it.

title: About
text:
Could it contain mistakes?
Yes, I am human and can make mistakes. If you spot an error or have a question about the data, email me with the details. I will correct any post containing verified errors and add a dated note at the top of the post saying what changed.

title: About
section: Why doesn’t it have social-platform buttons or comments?
text:
Why doesn’t it have social-platform buttons or comments?
Social-platform buttons load code from those platforms that lets them track readers, which is inconsistent with CWR’s privacy practices. The site and each post have a Share button offering a copy-able link or a pre-filled email, so it’s easy to share CWR content without loading any trackers. CWR has no accounts on any platform, and none are planned. And comments require moderation, which is too much effort for what is essentially a hobby blog.

title: About
section: How often will it contain new content?
text:
How often will it contain new content?
While I gain my bearings as a blogger, I’m going to under-promise and hopefully over-deliver. My initial aim is to publish two Snapshots and one Deep dive a month. Once I optimize my workflow and get used to writing for a general audience, I’ll likely up it to one Snapshot a week but keep it to a single Deep dive per month.

title: About
text:
Can I subscribe to it?
If you use an RSS reader, which aggregates articles from sites you like into a handy chronological feed, CWR’s feed is at https://chartingwaterlooregion.ca/index.xml. Your reader will also find it if you just give it chartingwaterlooregion.ca. If enough people start reading this blog and indicate they’d like another way to subscribe, I will consider wiring that feature into the site.

title: About
text:
How does it make money?
It doesn’t. Like Neil Young, it’s sponsored by nobody. CWR is a non-commercial venture, so it doesn’t have ads and it won’t ask you to pay for a subscription. If you find a post enlightening, hit the Like button or drop me an email. That’s all the reward I need.

title: Welcome to Charting Waterloo Region!
text:
My brother and I with our family’s first Mercury Montego, circa 1974.
As a kid, one of my favourite family activities was “going for a drive.” That is literally what we called it. Mom or Dad would announce that we were “going for a drive” and the five of us would pile into the Montego and go for a drive. A drive never had a destination, unless we ended up in Hespeler, where we’d get ice cream cones at a convenience store on Cooper Street. Almost all of them meandered through one or more of the Region’s townships. I particularly liked it when Dad drove through the Paradise Lake area in Wellesley Township. I thought it was neat that we had a little cottage-y area so close to home. These drives gave me an early appreciation for the Region’s vastness and variety, and for the contrasts between its rock ‘n’ roll heart and its country soul. In CWR’s inaugural post, we’ll start exploring some of these contrasts and, in the process, answer the burning question: “What do the townships have more of, cows or people?”

title: Welcome to Charting Waterloo Region!
section: An urban island in a sea of farmland
text:
An urban island in a sea of farmland
If you haven’t gone for many drives through the townships, you may have no idea how vast they are compared to the cities in the Region’s heart. On a map, they look like a giant jaw chomping the urban core they nearly surround. Collectively, the townships cover 1,056 square km, or 77% of the Region’s 1,370 square km. Even the smallest township, North Dumfries, is considerably larger than Kitchener, the biggest city.

title: Welcome to Charting Waterloo Region!
text:
More cows than people?!
You don’t have to drive through the townships to guess that they have fewer people than the cities, but do they have fewer people than cows? Before we answer that, let’s see how many more people live in the cities than in the townships.
The latest estimates from 2025 show that, with 323,917 residents, Kitchener has by far the highest population in the Region, slightly more than the other two cities combined. Together, the cities have 631,721 people, or 89% of the Region’s population of 711,457. So despite covering 77% of the Region’s territory, the townships are home to only 79,736 residents, or 11% of total population. With a combined density of only 75 residents per square km, they certainly have lots of room for cows!
   
By the way, cows did not figure in this post when I conceived it. Not until I saw the density data did I jokingly add the “More cows than people?!” heading to this section. And even after that, it took a while before I thought, I wonder if there actually is any data on how many cows there are in the townships. Serendipitously, I found that not only is there a Census of Population, there’s also a Census of Agriculture, which most non-farmers have probably never heard of. And when I dug into the most recent data from 2021, I was excited to learn that I could answer the question, “What do the townships have more of, cows or people?”
(In case there are any cattle farmers reading, I do know that cows are a specific type of cattle, along with heifers, steers, bulls, and calves. But to this lifelong city dweller, they are all cows, so when I say cows, I mean cattle.)
The population estimates above are for 2025, but the cow data is from 2021, so for a fair comparison, we’ll use the 2021 census populations as well. On census day in 2021, just over 70,000 people lived in the townships. How many cows lived in them on that day? Click the other tab to find out.

PeoplePeople and cows


   


   



And there we have it: more cows than people lived in the townships on census day in 2021. What I thought was a joke turns out to be true!

title: Welcome to Charting Waterloo Region!
text:
What have we learned?
In CWR’s debut post, we learned that my family thought it was fun to jump in our gas-guzzling Mercury and aimlessly roam the rural roads through the Region’s rolling hills. We learned there were lots of roads and hills to roam because the townships cover 1,056 square km, over three-quarters of the Region’s 1,370 square km, while holding only 79,736 people, a ninth of its 711,457 residents. And last, we learned that with so much space and so few residents, the townships were home to more cows than people in 2021. In future posts, we’ll explore more differences between the cities and their country cousins. And if CWR is still active a year or so from now, when this year’s census data is released, we’ll revisit this post and see if cows still outnumber people in cattle country.
